speechtext:
I must congratulate my hon. friend from Kamouraska, not only on the substance of the resolution he has introduced. but also on the manner in which he supported it. He has shown us that he has thoroughly studied the question, not only in its application to the Quebec district. but also to the whole Dominion. I 62i
have great pleasure in accepting the resolution, and hope that it will meet with the unanimous concurrence of the House. The resolution is in line with what was proposed two or three years ago.
Two or three years ago we put into the estimates a sum of money for the purpose of establishing branch stations on the experimental farm system. We have already acquired three such stations since that time, and I have been in negotiation with proprietors in other parts of the country with the object of securing suitable locations for other branch stations. I want to say that the requests which we have received from hon. members here to-day, and requests for such stations in different parts of the country, involve very large expenditures, and show great eagerness for the establishment of these stations. In deciding where we shall first do this work we have kept this principle in view, that the experimental stations should serve the largest number of people in a district which was a fair sample of a large area of country, rather thaif to establish stations m districts which should serve an area for a small population, or as a model of work of a restricted and peculiar character.

subtopic: EXPERIMENTAL FARMS ASKED FOE EASTERN QUEBEC.
speechtext: Would the minister say where the three stations are now ?

subtopic: EXPERIMENTAL FARMS ASKED FOE EASTERN QUEBEC.
speechtext:
One is in the semi dry district of southern Alberta, one is in the northern part of Alberta, and one in the northern part of Saskatchewan. Since the question has been asked, I will say why it was that these localities were first chosen for this work. In the original establishment of the experimental farm system, there were five farms established. There was the Central Experimental Farm here at Ottawa, which was expected to serve the purpose of Ontario and Quebec, lying as it does on the boundary line between them. One was near the boundary line between the province of New Brunswick and the province of Nova Scotia and within easy reach of Prince Edward Island, to serve the purposes of the maritime provinces. One was established in the then comparatively new province of Manitoba at Brandon; a fourth was established at Indian Head in the then new territory further west, and a fifth was established in the great province of British Columbia. The idea was that these stations should serve the provinces mentioned. When, however, a few years ago we established two new provinces In the Northwest, we found that the province of Alberta had no farm which seemed to serve the needs of that great agricultural province. The question was how we could meet these needs, and instead of establishing a branch farm at some central point for the whole province, as was done in the earlier scheme

of organization, we thought better to establish two smaller stations, one in the south part, which is dryer, and one in the more central part of that great agricultural province, nearer the northern region, where farming must necessarily be of a mixed character, and where conditions are different from those at Lethbridge, where the southern farm was established.

subtopic: EXPERIMENTAL FARMS ASKED FOE EASTERN QUEBEC.
speechtext: How many acres were acquired for the experimental farm in the northern part?

subtopic: EXPERIMENTAL FARMS ASKED FOE EASTERN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I will not go into details of that kind just now.

subtopic: EXPERIMENTAL FARMS ASKED FOE EASTERN QUEBEC.
speechtext: Perhaps the minister will tell us when these new farms were established?

subtopic: EXPERIMENTAL FARMS ASKED FOE EASTERN QUEBEC.
speechtext:
As soon as possible after the establishment of the province of Alberta. I think I acquired the first one about two years ago, and the second one a little over a year ago, immediately after the province of Alberta was established. Now a third farm was established in the northern part of Saskatchewan, very much for the same reason that the two farms were established in Alberta. The farm at Indian Head, in Saskatchewan, is in the southern part of the province on the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, where the land is altogether prairie, where the climate is rather dry, and where farming consisted in wheat growing. We wish to establish another farm in the northern part where wood land is mixed with prairie land, and where the syle of agriculture will be necessarily different from that in the southern part. For that purpose we have bought a farm at Rosthern, between Saskatoon and Prince Albert. I have been in negotiation with the provincial governments of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island with a view to their purchasing a farm each, and placing it at our disposal for this work. We have not yet been able to fix upon the exact location, but I believe that before long these governments will be able to place at our disposal for the purpose of carrying on such work as this, one farm in the fruitgrowing district of Nova Scotia, and another in the centre of Prince Edward Island. I have had many applications for the enlargement of this system, and I wish to continue in the line that we have begun. I may say that I have already promised that a farm shall be established on the island of Vancouver, in British Columbia. The conditions there are very different, from an agricultural point of view, from the condtions on the mainland, and it seems only fair and right that that great island should have a model station where experiments and illustrations of the best agricultural methods can be carried on. My hon. friend from Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve), and my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell), Mr. FISHER.
have spoken of the interior or dry belt of the province of British Columbia. Here let me say to those gentlemen from British Columbia that no district in the Dominion has been given more careful consideration and study than the mainland of the province of British Columbia, both on my own part and on the part of my officials.
Most of us know pretty well the general character of that great province, but probably none of us realize its immense agricultural possibilities. The beauty of its scenery is famed the world over, as are the richness of its mineral resources and its wealth of fisheries, but I venture to say that in the future it will be the agriculture and the fruit growing of British Columbia of which Canada will be most proud, and from which it will reap the greatest advantages. I dare say it is a surprise to many to learn that there are 75,000 acres of orchard land in that province, and while many of the trees are not yet bearing, still so great has been the profit accruing that in recent years there have been thousands of acres of fruit trees planted and the experience already has proven that those who have engaged in the industry have been wise in their generation. There is a difficulty in the way, however. The country i3 divided by mountain chains and ridges, and the crop which is suitable to one valley may not be suitable to any very wide area. It is therefore impossible to find one central spot in the interior of British Columbia where an experimental farm or illustration station could be established to serve the whole of the interior. Until the time comes when such stations will be numerous, we will have to proceed on the principle of selecting a site which will serve the largest area and the greatest number of agriculturists within reasonable reach of the centre. In most other parts of Canada an illustration or experimental station will serve a- very large area and to begin with it is well that we should place them where they will be of benefit to the greatest number of people. I have been guided as much as possible by this consideration in the order in which I have taken up the placing of these experimental stations. I would like to go much further in this direction than I have gone. Let me tell hon. gentlemen who have not been many years in this House a little bit of history. In the year 1899 I came forward with a proposition in regard to illustration stations somewhat smaller than those branch experimental stations, and I desired as time went on and as I was allowed to have money enough to do it, to establish such a station in every county of the Dominion. And after eight years experience of the results of that proposition not having been given effect to, I have no hesitation in saying that the loss has been enormous to the agriculturists of Canada. But, the House of Commons was opposed to my

proposition and it had to be withdrawn, and from that day to this I have not undertaken to reintroduce it. I hope, however, that my idea will be amplified as time goes on, until, if not in every county of the Dominion, at all events in every part of the Dominion where an experimental station may serve a large number of agriculturists,, we shall have one established. I am glad to hear my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) and other hon. gentlemen approve of the stations already established. I can endorse what my hon. friend from South Alberta (Mr. Magrath) said as to the effects of the experimental farm at Indian Head. The district of Indian Head is probably to-day the most productive of that great whea't growing region, and I only speak what I have heard said by hundreds and hundreds of the best judges in the Northwest when I say that the fact that the Indian Head district is to-day so much in advance of most parts of the Northwest is due to the establishment of the experimental farm station there. I venture to say that everybody who knows the great wheat growing prairie area between the great lakes and the Rocky mountains will endorse my statement that Mr. McKay, the manager of the Indian Head farm, has done more to educate the farmers of the Northwest in the proper methods of wheat growing than any other dozen or perhaps any other hundred men in the Dominion of Canada. His work in that direction has been largely assisted by the fact that at Indian Head he has been able to carry on careful experimentation and observation, the results of which he has for a long term of years placed before the farmers of the Northwest. I believe that the, same can be said for the experimental farm at Brandon and other farms throughout the country. My hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder) spoke about the value to the farmers of the evidence taken before 4he select committee on agriculture and he seemed to complain that this literature was not as freely circulated as it might be. Well, that is for the Committee of Agriculture and the Committee on Printing to deal with, because the taking of that evidence and the distribution of it is entirely under the control of the members of this House, and the Department of Agriculture and the Minister of Agriculture have nothing to do with it. If the evidence is not sent out to the farmers of Canada it is because the members of the House do not take the trouble to send it out.

subtopic: EXPERIMENTAL FARMS ASKED FOE EASTERN QUEBEC.
speechtext: The difficulty is that such a long time elapses before it is printed.

subtopic: EXPERIMENTAL FARMS ASKED FOE EASTERN QUEBEC.
speechtext:
That defect can be remedied by the Committee on Printing and the Committee on Agriculture. I have no more control over that as Minister of Agriculture than my hon. friend has. I have inveighed against it, and urged the Committee on Agriculture to take steps with regard to it, but effective steps have not yet been taken.
Now, let me say a word with regard to some remarks of my hon., friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell). He spoke of irrigation and said that nothing had been done by the Department of Agriculture to measure the water that was required for the irrigating of certain lands. Let me say that in the establishment of the experimental station at Lethbridge a little more than two years ago that very work was taken up. Mr. Fairfield, the manager of that station, is an expert in irrigation work, and one of the first things that was laid out for him was that he should establish gates and measures on the irrigation canals of that farm, and watch them and take notes, and find out as quickly as possible the very point my hon. friend asked for. It is true, these gates and measures and sluices have only been built a little less than a year. They were erected as soon as possible after we acquired the farm, and therefore we have no results yet which we can place before the public; but just as soon as it is possible to obtain the results, they will be made available for those who wish to carry on irrigation work. Nobody appreciates more than myself the immense value of irrigation work in semi-arid or dry parts of our country. That has been impressed upon me for years, both in regard to that large area of land in the interior of British Columbia and that large area in southern Alberta and southern Saskatchewan, which until quite recently was thought to be too dry for agricultural experiments. I am glad to say that discoveries have been made by which to-day it is well known that much of that dry land can be cultivated, under methods which any farmer can carry on, and that excellent crops are assured in those parts of the country without irrigation. Irrigation is a splendid adjunct and help to that kind of dry farming. On the station at Lethbridge just that kind of work is being experimented with, and just as soon as we have any results that are assured, that information will be given to the public. If there is one thing in connection with the experimental farm system of Canada of which I am proud, and of which everybody connected with agriculture in Canada may be proud, it is that Dr. Saunders, who is at the head of that system, is a man of scientific attainments, well trained in scientific agricultural experimental work, a man who hesitates to jump to conclusions, but who, as soon as the conclusions have been scien-tificially proved, is well able to put them clearly and concisely, so that the ordinary farmer can understand them; and it has been the glory of that system, that what has been concluded as the results of years

of experiment, and what has been put before the public, has been universally acknowledged to be correct and well founded. Dr. Saunders and bis staff have never yet been obliged to withdraw any point that they have put forward, and have never been found out in hasty or incorrect conclusions. I congratulate Canada, and I congratulate myself as the minister in charge of that particular work, that we have a man of scientific training and attainments on whose word we can thoroughly and absolutely rely as to the results of his experiments.
Let me say, too, in reply to my hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder), that while he is correct in saying that science must be joined with practice, still without science-and science to be of any use must be full and clear-the work of the practical farmer would be much less efficient than it is to-day in Canada. It was only a few weeks ago that in this city of Ottawa, and in these buildings, there was held the annual meeting of the Seed Grain Growers Association, and I regret extremely that more members of the House did not take part in that meeting. Dr. Robertson, the head of the McDonald Agricultural College at St. Anne, delivered an address in which he put before the meeting the fact that if the fields of grain in the province of Quebec generally had produced as much per acre as the fields of grain on the McDonald College farm, they would have produced $100,000,000 worth more than the grain crops of Quebec last year amounted to. That was not the quantity raised on the experimental plots, but was the quantity raised on some two hundred acres of the McDonald College farm. This is a statement of startling importance; and I venture to say, in reply to the hon. member from Dundas, that scientific knowledge is the handmaid of practical agriculture. Without scientific knowledge practical agriculture cannot make those advances in our country and on this continent which its importance justifies. The farmers of Canada today, partly through the experimental farm system, partly through the operations of the other branches of my department, and partly through the work of the different branches of agriculture in the various provinces, have an abundance of knowledge at their disposal which they do not make full use of. If they would make use of one-tenth of it and carry one-hun-dreth part of it into their everyday operations, the results would amount to tens of millions of dollars more from agricultural produce than there is to-day. It is the farmer's slip-shod methods in this country which is the limit of our agricultural production. We are fortunate in Canada in having established a reputation in the world's market for a fine quality of agricultural product; and today the market of Great Britain and Ireland is reaching out Mr. FISHER.
and demanding more of our finished agricultural products than we are sending to it, and the prices we get for these articles which we do send are such as to give the farmers of this country who raise the goods and export them splendid profits and splendid results, and the only pity is that the farmers of Canada are not doubling and quadrupling their exports every year. If they do not do it, it is not for lack of teaching or for lack of knowledge; it is for their lack of interest in their work, their lack of industry, and largely, I believe, for, the lack of that labour which is necessary in the carrying on of our farming operations.
Sir, the experimental farm system has, for twenty odd years back, been laying before the farmers knowledge of an inestimable value. Many have taken advantage of it, many have improved their methods as a result of it; enough have done so to be a leaven that is working through the whole system of agriculture in the country. There has been enormous progress, there has been great improvement and the agriculture of Canada to-day is infinitely ahead of what it was twenty years ago when the experimental farm system was first established. This is largely due to the example and model of these farms. It is largely due to the experiments which have been carried on, the principal results of which have been sent broadcast among the people through reports and bulletins, that this progress and improvement are so great. I venture to think that we can safely and wisely multiply the number of illustration stations so that the farmers who do not read and do not quite apprehend all that they do read may be able to go easily to these stations and see what they can do. Then I think they would be more willing to go home and try to follow up what they have seen. I would be glad, if, within seeing reach of every farmer in the Dominion, there was an experimental plot, or rather, I would like to call it an illustration plot, where, he could see the best methods in regard to those crops which are best adapted to the region in which he lives, so that the eye, as well as the comprehension in reading, will teach him what to do. It is a big and broad subject and the undertaking is too much to be accomplished in one year or perhaps in ten years, but we ought to work towards that end, and the resolution which my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) has introduced is a confirmation of my own opinion and an encouragement to me to go on and try to carry out as much as possible of the system which I had already inaugurated and which I would	like to	amplify'	- ,	.	,	,Let me say	]ust one word	m	regard	to apoint that I	had in mind. Different	sections of the country have organized excursions to the experimental farms in other parts of the country as well as to the ex-
perimental farm here. A very good thing. We have had some of the most interested and _ most intelligent bodies of farmers coming from the province of Quebec to the Central Experimental Farm, among them men who have come as far as 400 or 500 miles and spent three or four days on the trip so as to be able to have an opportunity of seeing the work on that farm and of going home with a better understanding of what farming is in a scientific way. I may say that I have had abundant evidence of this fact. I have letters by the score and by the hundreds from these people congratulating the Department of Agriculture on what was being done at the Central Experimental Farm, letters, which have, in consequence of these visits, even anticipated my hon. friend from Kamouraska and other hon. gentlemen who have asked for the establishment of other experimental stations. This is the best evidence of the value of these experimental stations, and I am glad to know that these excursions have taken place in different parts of the country. In Nova Scotia, Cape Breton and Prince Edward Island farmers have organized excursions to Nappan, out in the west, in the province of Manitoba, excursions are held to Brandon; in Saskatchewan and Alberta to Indian Head, and I believe also in British Columbia there are excursions of those interested in the fruit growing industry to Agassiz.
Let me say one word in reply to the remarks of my hon. friend from Yale-Carihoo (Mr. Burrell) in that connection. He spoke of the work there as being no use to the interior dry belt. I agree with him that it is of very little use. It happens that Agassiz is a very wet place and the result is that the work of fruit growing there is of very little value from the experimental point of, view to the dry belt of British Columbia. The farm is so situated that it is almost impossible to keep live stock on it successfully and well. The result is that the farm has not been of that advantage to British Columbia which was expected, and which, I think, a farm of that kind ought to be. That is one reason why I immediately decided that I would put a farm on the Island of Vancouver and why I have been groping and trying to find the right place to put an experimental station in the dry belt of the province. An hon. gentleman spoke about protection against insect pests and diseases which attack fruit trees, &c. Our farm system has been working on that ever since its inception. Let me here say that one of the very best officers of the experimental farm system was the late lamented Dr. Fletcher, entymologist and botanist of the experimental farm. His reputation and work extended far beyond the limits of Canada. He inaugurated economic botany and entymology, which is the true application of these two great natural sciences to the practical work of the farm, and his work has told so well that Canada is today freer of insect pests than any other country, which produces so much fruit and has so many trees. It is true that in a small portion of Ontario the San Jose scale is planted and established. That occurred some years ago, but our measures to shut out nursery stock and seedlings coming in from the United States, which is infested with this scale without fumigation, have been so successful that this pest has not been introduced into any part of Canada where it was not then in existence. It is true that it is spreading a little in that portion of Ontario where it has existed for so long. Efforts have been made to control it and reduce its evil effects.. The provincial government has been acting in this direction and I believe to-day that while the work has not been altogether successful it is largely due to the efforts of the provincial government that the pest has not spread much more widely and that it has not covered those parts of the province where the fruits which it affects are produced. We must beware of other pests. Just at this present moment Dr. Saunders and his staff are watching and fighting against the introduction into parts of Canada where it is not yet known of an insect which is known as the brown tailed moth, a pest which has attacked the great state of New York and other states on the border and is creating the utmost havoc amongst fruit and other trees. That pest is known slightly in our own maritime provinces. We are taking steps to stimulate its extermination there and we are watching and examining every entry of fruit trees and seedlings coming into Canada from those countries where this pest exists, so as to make sure that the pest will not be introduced into this country. That is but one instance of the work that the farm system is doing to protect this great fruit growing industry.
My hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) said a few words a little while ago about spraying materials. I commend his views with regard to the free entry of spraying materials, and I can only congratulate him, myself and the House on the fact that so ardent a protectionist as he is is willing to reduce the duties or remove them from any item. I am glad to hear it and I can assure him that he has my entire sympathy. I have spoken perhaps too long, but I feel very strongly on this subject. I think that I am in a better position than most men to know what has been the advantage of such work as the experimental farm stations and similar stations can do in this country. I have no hesitation at all in saying that what little expenditure Canada has made in this way has been returned, not only to the farmers,

but to every man, woman and child within the boundaries of the Dominion, ten and twenty times over in the results which have been achieved; and I am satisfied that any further expenditure, even running into large sums if we are able, with the present declining revenue to spend, the money will be equally well returned to the whole country. Do not imagine for a moment, Mr. Speaker, that this is a question which affects the farmers only. It affects the whole country; it affects the transportation interest, the mercantile interests, the export trade and the import trade. If, in any way, we can accomplish even one-tenth of what Dr. Robertson said could be accomplished in the province of Quebec simply in one part of the work of improving agriqulture-the improvement in the seed grain-we shall deserve well of our country, and I am sure that future generations will arise and call us blessed.

subtopic: EXPERIMENTAL FARMS ASKED FOE EASTERN QUEBEC.
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, we have just heard a most interesting debate and I am not surprised, I admit, at the promise which has just been made on behalf of the government. I expected a precise statement from the hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), for although this question may appear a new one in certain respects, in others it is not so. I well remember having referred to it in this House during the last parliament and having laid before the government the same request as that made to-day by the member for Kamour-aska, for the establishment in the province of Quebec of a very unpretending experimental farm, not nearly so extensive as the central farm at Ottawa, but sufficient nevertheless to supply our farmers with that information which it is difficult for them to obtain from our central station. I entered into no details as to its situation or extent. I stated before the House that we had spent much for the experimental farms so far established and that in view of the various conditions obtaining throughout our vast territory, this expenditure, great though it had been, was yet inadequate to the wants of the different provinces. I requested the minister to establish in the province of Quebec a model farm which would be within the reach of all the inhabitants of that province, and so conducted that farmers speaking the French language might be enabled to reap every possible benefit therefrom.
It is a great satisfaction to me to find that the minister has considerably altered his views concerning such stations, for when I made that request, urging practically the same arguments and giving the same statistics which have been to-day adduced before the House, I could not secure his approval. I predicted that he would become a convert Mr. FISHER.
to public opinion and I now find that he has been reclaimed.
No doubt, I would have desired more explicit explanations on the part of the minister as to the location of the farm to be built in compliance with the wishes of the hon. member for Kamouraska. The question being one of long standing and having been several times submitted to the Minister of Agriculture, who now admits that the step is necessary, we had a right to expect from him something more positive concerning the establishment he intends to create in the eastern portion of Quebec.
After the harmonious debate of this afternoon, I have certainly no intention of striking a discordant note, but I will say that in view of the great development of experimental farms in the Northwest, we are entitled to require a little more than this for the province of Quebec. There are already three experimental farms in that region of comparatively recent development. The minister has to-day declared that he has considered it necessary to establish no less than two new farms in Alberta and one in Saskatchewan. He informs us that another will soon be in operation in British Columbia. Now what arguments are we in a position to bring up in support of the motion now before the House? Have we not the Lake St. John region, containing at least a million acres of farming land upon which hundreds of rich and prosperous parishes might be built up? Have we not also the ancient valley of the St. Lawrence, concerning which our data are very general and vague and which is generally supposed to be so poor that the farmers living there scarcely reap a sufficiency? Nothing could be more removed from the truth, the regiop being exceedingly rich, but its various climates require to be studied. It is well known that fruit-growing has been undertaken with excellent results to the east of the city of Quebec. Have we not, moreover the valley of the Metapedia, where settlement is well advanced and which would be benefited by an experimental farm in eastern Quebec?
I am gratified to find that opinions which I claim as having been the first to express them here, are to-day unanimously accepted, even by the minister who some years ago had not attained the conviction which he has proclaimed to-day. Shall we have that experimental farm, and when?
There seems to be, I regret to find, some difference of opinion, even among the representatives of the region, as to the proper location of the experimental farm. The member for Quebec claims it for his constituency.

Let our farmers be given the same opportunities of progressing, let means of education be extended to them as generously as they are to others, and I am convinced that that exceedingly intelligent portion of our fellow countrymen will be even more prompt in taking advantage of them than many other portions of the population of Canada. I have acquired this conviction while travelling through the province of Quebec.
I would advise my friends in the Quebec district to elect a few more members to sit on the opposition side of the House. That would perhaps help them in obtaining experimental farms of which the government is so profuse in the west. How can the thing be explained unless by the indifference of the government? My hon. friend may indeed desire to punish those whom he loves and according to the principle of the Good Shepherd, he may be willing to leave the faithful flock, to go off in search of the stray lambs. I cannot tell; but apparently it is to the advantage of certain portions of the country not to pay too humble a court to the powers that be.

speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I will add but a few words to the speech of my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture. As to the somewhat acerb remarks of the member for Jacques Cartier, I may pass them over in consideration of the cordial support he has given to the motion submitted by * the nember for Kamouraska.
The latter deserves to be congratulated upon the eloquent and instructive speech he has delivered, a speech showing that he has seriously studied the question. My hon. friend's success has been the more remarkable that opinions are generally so sharply divided here. He has rallied every representative in this House from Halifax to Vancouver to the idea that we have so long entertained of establishing an experimental farm in the district of Quebec. Montreal cannot object to such a request which is of more or less local interest. Indeed Montreal is within three hours journey of the excellent experimental farm we have here in Ottawa. Moreover, the whole Montreal region will reap especial benefit from the great agricultural school lately founded in the province of Quebec by that distinguished Scotchman, Sir William McDonald. The Oka school also will be of great use to the district of Montreal. But Quebec is far removed from Ottawa and from those schools. The climate of Quebec, as is well known,
differs from that of Montreal. Even within the Quebec district important variations of climate may be observed. Thus, in Gaspe and Bonaventure, the winter is longer than in Quebec, but milder. Summer and autumn lasts three and sometimes four weeks more.
We of Bonaventure and Gaspe have no present intention of claiming an experimental farm. The Quebec district proper should, we think, take precedence; that is one of the clearest results of the motion made this afternoon by my hon. friend from Kamouraska.
The member for Jacques Cartier does not seem convinced of the government's good faith in this matter. He even claims that if the district of Quebec should obtain an experimental farm, it will be due to his own efforts. I know that during the last session certain questions were asked concerning this, but I think I am not mistaken when I say that during the last election the people of the Quebec region themselves delivered to their representatives an imperative mandate to have so important a question definitely settled.
The member for Kamouraska deserves our thanks for having taken this matter in hand, and also our congratulations for hav ing succeeded in carrying conviction to both sides of the House. He has been through out the spokesman of the district of Quebec and has obtained from the Minister of Agriculture the equivalent of an official promise that his views will be promptly carried out.
